name: Question 13
worked_solution:
By the chain rule, we have 

$$
(g∘u)^{′}(t)=g′(u(t))u′(t)
$$

Now, let's find the derivatives of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(u) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\operatorname{ln}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}0,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\frac{1}{u})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{u},\,0,\,-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}⟩ \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})=2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(g∘u)^{′}(t) & =g′(u(t))u′(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{u(t)},\,0,\,-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}(t)}⟩{u}^{′}(t) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}⟨\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}},\,0,\,-\frac{1}{({e}^{2t})^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{e}^{2t}}{{e}^{2t}},\,0,\,-\frac{2{e}^{2t}}{{e}^{4t}}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,-2{e}^{-2t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

If g(u)=⟨ln⁡u,0,1u⟩ and u(t)=e2t, then (g∘u)′(t)=

a
⟨e−2t,0,e−4t⟩
b
⟨e−2t,0,−e−4t⟩
c
⟨2,0,−2e2t⟩
d
⟨2,0,−2e−2t⟩
e
⟨2,0,2e2t⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

By the chain rule, we have (g∘u)′(t)=g′(u(t))u′(t)

Now, let's find the derivatives of each function: g′(u)=⟨dduln⁡u,ddu0,ddu(1u)⟩=⟨1u,0,−1u2⟩u′(t)=ddt(e2t)=2e2t Therefore, we obtain:

(g∘u)′(t)=g′(u(t))u′(t)=⟨1u(t),0,−1u2(t)⟩u′(t)=2e2t⟨1e2t,0,−1(e2t)2⟩=⟨2e2te2t,0,−2e2te4t⟩=⟨2,0,−2e−2t⟩
